title: After My Clinical Clerkships in the UK
paragraphs: For two months from March 2025, I was given a valuable opportunity for clinical clerkships in the UK. I did my clerkships mainly in breast surgery at Newcastle University and in the emergency department at the University of Edinburgh, and I also visited General Practice (GP) in Glasgow for a short time. It was a clerkship in which I gained much learning about a healthcare system different from Japan's, the attitudes of the doctors and medical staff working in the field, and relationships with patients.

Newcastle is located in the north of England and is a lively city where industry and academia coexist. In March there were still days with snow flurries, and with the winter cold lingering, I took part in a four-week breast surgery clerkship at the Royal Victoria Infirmary (RVI).

In Japan, breast surgeons often handle everything consistently from diagnosis to surgery, drug therapy and even end-of-life care, whereas in the UK, as a breast care team, breast surgeons, radiologists, medical oncologists, pathologists, GPs and others clearly divide roles, and team medicine that makes use of each specialty is practiced. A multidisciplinary conference was held every Friday, and treatment policy was discussed enthusiastically over three to four hours.

What was impressive was the efficiency and rationality of surgery. A continuous flow was established in which a patient who has been put under general anesthesia in the anesthetic room enters the operating room, moves immediately to the recovery room after surgery, and the next patient is brought in still asleep, so the turnover rate of the operating rooms was very high and up to five operations were sometimes performed in the same room in one day. Also, many patients finished surgery as day cases and went home even with a drain in place, which gave me a new perspective on how surgical care can be.

There were also many patients who placed importance on appearance, and operations to reduce the healthy breast after tumor removal and simultaneous reconstruction were performed routinely. I learned a lot about the variety of surgical techniques and about what care should be like to raise patients' QOL.

The atmosphere was also very open to exchange students, and in the clerkship I did outpatient observation, pre-visit history taking, assisting in operations, observation of the pathology department, and helping with biopsies and mammography in radiology. The doctors had an attitude of actively letting students experience procedures, and I was actually allowed to experience many. For me, who aims at breast surgery in the future, being able to touch actual practice in another country at the front line of clinical care was a valuable experience directly connected to my future career.

Edinburgh, which I visited next, is also called the town of Harry Potter, a beautiful city of history and culture, and I was impressed by its calm atmosphere that suits light rain. I did my clerkship in the Walk-in emergency department of the Royal Infirmary of Edinburgh.

In the UK, under the NHS (National Health Service) system, in the emergency department a decision of "admit or go home" must be made within four hours of reception. The doctors on site therefore looked very busy, but even so I was impressed by their educational attitude of carefully providing me, an exchange student, with chances to take histories and time to think together about evaluating images and test results. My role was to pick up the files of patient information piled up one after another, call the patient into a booth and take the pre-visit history and physical findings. Because it was a more practical clerkship, there were times I agonized over my lack of knowledge, but thanks to the doctors' warm guidance I think I grew a great deal.

I also negotiated by myself and was allowed to observe the breast surgery department located in the next building. I sincerely thank the doctors and nurses who accepted me. In Edinburgh too, reconstruction operations were performed very frequently, and it was very valuable to be able to see almost daily operations, such as fat grafting and simultaneous reconstruction, that I had been able to observe only a few times in Japan.

I was also given the opportunity to meet Dr. Logan, a GP in Glasgow who has deep ties with Nagoya University. At his clinic I was able to observe up close the reality of community medicine handling a wide range of diseases, from a child's cold symptoms to follow-up after test results at the university hospital. I was able to hear from him what kind of medicine he wants to provide to patients as a GP. Coming into contact with a style of practice that, unlike at large hospitals, values trust with each patient, was an opportunity to reconfirm the significance of holistic medicine.

In the UK, medical costs are covered by taxes, and the NHS strictly manages access to healthcare so that all citizens can receive the same standard of care fairly. GPs play the role of gatekeepers, and a GP's referral letter is needed to access advanced medical facilities such as university hospitals. At first glance it is a system that gives the impression of being "hard to see a doctor," but high-priority diseases are dealt with quickly, for example with a guarantee of an examination within 35 days for patients diagnosed with cancer, and I felt that the system is devised so as to allocate medical resources appropriately.

I was also impressed that simplification of clerical work is advanced, that chart entry by voice input and electronic medical record information are shared with the patients themselves through the NHS app, and that information is coordinated between hospitals even without referral letters. I too actually experienced voice input and was surprised at its accuracy.

There were also many points worth noting about how doctors work. They begin work around 8 in the morning and leave at 17:00 in the evening, taking leave by the week is also common, and a culture in which doctors work with a good balance, valuing their family and their own time, is firmly rooted. I strongly felt that, even in Japan, which faces a society with a declining birthrate and an aging population and increasing numbers of patients, medical resources and the working environment need to be reconsidered.

I am truly happy that I have been able to finish safely the clinical study abroad that I set as a goal from when I entered university. I am convinced that the knowledge and broadened perspective gained through this clerkship will certainly be put to use as the foundation of my life as a doctor. Because Newcastle University was a non-partner school and the University of Edinburgh was a first-time dispatch this year, there was little information beforehand, and I had no friend from Nagoya University with me, so there were times I felt forlorn. My English, in which I had confidence, also sometimes could not get across what I wanted to ask in the real clinical setting, and I felt frustrated at not being able to keep up with the speed of patients and doctors. However, thanks to the kindness of the patients, doctors, nurses and medical staff who warmly welcomed me, an exchange student, and spoke to me, I think I was able to have a fruitful two months of clerkships. A receptionist who, when I was wandering lost in the hospital, immediately spoke to me and took me to my destination; a patient who, during the pre-visit history, got into travel talk with "You're from Nagoya? I've been to Nagoya too"; a patient who, when I was sitting at the nurse station of the emergency department, called out from the bed and let me auscultate the sound of their pacemaker; an operating room nurse who messaged me recommended sightseeing spots and restaurants saying "You're in the operating room on such a nice day? Edinburgh has lovely places"; and so on. It was two months surrounded by the kindness of many people. There were hard times, such as assisting in four or five operations every day from 8 to 17 and aiming for gaps among the busy doctors to give presentations, but by speaking up and taking part in clerkships on my own initiative, I was allowed to take on new things one after another.
Finally, I would like to thank everyone who gave me the valuable opportunity to learn. Thank you.
